title: Pandas Groupby and Summaries: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of split-apply-combine in pandas: groupby with agg, multiple and named aggregations, transform vs agg, pivot_table, value_counts and crosstab. Covers the mental model, workflow, everyday usage, common mistakes and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Split-Apply-Combine Mental Model
points: Definition: split rows into groups by key, apply a function to each group, combine the results into one object
df.groupby('city') only builds a lazy DataFrameGroupBy object; nothing is computed until you call an aggregation, transform, apply or iterate
Example: df.groupby('city')['sales'].sum() returns a Series indexed by city, with one row per group
The apply step has three result shapes: aggregate (one row per group), transform (same length as input), filter (keeps or drops whole groups)
Interview Point: What are the three steps of split-apply-combine? Why is groupby lazy? What shape does each apply type return?

chapters.title: Core Workflow: groupby with agg
points: Pick the key(s), select the column(s), then choose the aggregation: df.groupby(['city','year'])['sales'].mean()
Multiple keys give a MultiIndex result; as_index=False or .reset_index() turns the keys back into columns
Multiple aggregations on one column: df.groupby('city')['sales'].agg(['sum','mean','count'])
Named aggregation gives clean column names: .agg(total=('sales','sum'), avg=('sales','mean'), n=('id','count'))
Interview Point: How do you apply different functions to different columns? What is named aggregation? What does as_index=False do?

chapters.title: transform vs agg vs apply
points: agg reduces each group to a scalar, so the result has one row per group
transform returns a result aligned to the original index (same length as df), so it can be assigned straight back as a column
Example: df['pct'] = df['sales'] / df.groupby('city')['sales'].transform('sum') gives each row's share of its group total
transform also handles group-wise fill and standardise: transform(lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std())
Interview Point: When do you use transform instead of agg? What does transform guarantee about the index? Why is a built-in aggregation name faster than a lambda or apply?

chapters.title: pivot_table, value_counts and crosstab
points: pivot_table(index='city', columns='year', values='sales', aggfunc='sum') is groupby plus unstack: it reshapes a grouped summary into a grid
pivot_table options: aggfunc accepts a list or dict, fill_value=0 replaces NaN, margins=True adds an 'All' row and column
value_counts() counts the unique values of a Series, sorted descending; normalize=True gives proportions and dropna=False keeps NaN
pd.crosstab(df['city'], df['plan']) counts the combinations of two categoricals; normalize='index' gives row percentages
Interview Point: pivot_table vs crosstab: when to use which? How does value_counts relate to groupby().size()? What is pivot vs pivot_table?

chapters.title: Common Mistakes
points: groupby drops NaN keys by default; use dropna=False to keep them as their own group
count() skips NaN values while size() counts all rows, so the two can disagree
Using apply or a lambda where a built-in aggregation exists is much slower on large data
groupby('k').agg('sum') aggregates every non-key column (text columns raise or concatenate); select the value columns explicitly, e.g. groupby('k')['v'].agg('sum')
Interview Point: Why can group counts not match the row count? How would you speed up a slow groupby? What does a MultiIndex result need to become flat columns?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Groupby and Summaries
points: Aggregate: df.groupby('k')['v'].agg(['sum','mean']) or .agg(total=('v','sum'))
Broadcast back: df['x'] = df.groupby('k')['v'].transform('mean')
Grid summary: df.pivot_table(index='a', columns='b', values='v', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0, margins=True)
Counts: s.value_counts(normalize=True) and pd.crosstab(df.a, df.b, normalize='index')

Interview Point: Pick the right tool: agg for one row per group, transform for same-length output, pivot_table for a value grid, crosstab for category counts, value_counts for one column's frequencies
